whyNext: Builds on node degree counting from Course Schedule (Seq 212) by identifying the central node of a star graph through edge intersection of just the first two edges in O(1) time.
hints: In a star graph, the center node is connected to every single other node in the graph.
Therefore, the center node must appear in every edge.
Comparing just the first two edges edges[0] and edges[1]: the node common to both edges is the center.

brute.idea: Count the degrees of all nodes across all edges and find the node with degree == n - 1.
steps: Create an int array degree of size n + 1.
For each edge [u, v]: degree[u]++, degree[v]++.
Scan degree array for index with degree == edges.length.
Return that node.
brute.whySlow: Iterates through all edges when comparing just the first two suffices.

optimal.idea: Two-edge intersection: the node appearing in both edges[0] and edges[1] is guaranteed to be the center in O(1) time.
steps: Look at edges[0] = [u1, v1] and edges[1] = [u2, v2].
If u1 == u2 or u1 == v2 return u1.
Otherwise return v1.

whyNext: Builds on node degree properties from Find Center of Star Graph (Seq 443) by computing net trust degrees (inDegree - outDegree) to locate the unique individual with score equal to n - 1.
hints: The town judge trusts nobody (outDegree == 0).
Everybody else trusts the town judge (inDegree == n - 1).
Combine both into a single net trust array: score = inDegree - outDegree. The town judge has score == n - 1.

brute.idea: Track separate in-degree and out-degree arrays, then find person with in-degree n-1 and out-degree 0.
steps: Create inDegree and outDegree arrays of size n + 1.
For each trust pair [a, b]: outDegree[a]++; inDegree[b]++;
Loop i from 1 to n: if inDegree[i] == n - 1 and outDegree[i] == 0, return i.
Return -1.
brute.whySlow: Uses two separate arrays when one net degree array suffices.

optimal.idea: Single net degree array: increment score for incoming trust and decrement for outgoing trust in O(E + n) time.
steps: int[] score = new int[n + 1].
For each trust [a, b]: score[a]--; score[b]++;
Loop i from 1 to n: if score[i] == n - 1 return i.
Return -1.

whyNext: Builds on directed graph in-degree evaluation from Find the Town Judge (Seq 444) by identifying all vertices with in-degree 0, which must be in any valid starting set since they cannot be reached from any other node.
hints: Any node that has no incoming edges (in-degree == 0) cannot be reached from any other vertex.
Therefore, every node with in-degree == 0 must be included in the starting set.
In a DAG, all nodes with in-degree > 0 can be reached from some node with in-degree == 0. So the answer is simply all nodes with in-degree == 0.

brute.idea: Run BFS from every subset of nodes to check if they reach all n vertices.
steps: Track in-degrees of all nodes.
Filter nodes with in-degree == 0.
Verify reachability with BFS.
Return list of zero in-degree nodes.
brute.whySlow: Running verification BFS is redundant since zero in-degree nodes are provably necessary and sufficient in a DAG.

optimal.idea: Boolean in-degree array: mark targets of directed edges; return all indices that remain unmarked in O(V + E) time.
steps: boolean[] hasIncoming = new boolean[n].
For each edge [u, v]: hasIncoming[v] = true.
List<Integer> ans = new ArrayList<>().
For i from 0 to n - 1: if !hasIncoming[i] ans.add(i).
Return ans.

whyNext: Builds on directed tree edge tracking from Minimum Number of Vertices to Reach All Nodes (Seq 445) by building an undirected adjacency list with directional flags, counting edges directed away from root 0 that must be reversed.
hints: Represent original edges as directed, but build an undirected graph so you can traverse outward from city 0 to every other city.
When moving outward from 0: if the original edge went from parent to child (away from 0), it must be reversed (cost 1).
Store neighbors with cost: (neighbor, 1) if edge u -> v, and (neighbor, 0) if edge v -> u. Run BFS/DFS from 0 and sum costs.

brute.idea: Construct adjacency lists and run DFS from 0, checking edge direction against a set of original edges.
steps: Store original edges in a HashSet of strings "u->v".
Build undirected tree graph.
DFS from 0: if moving across an edge in set, increment change count.
Return change count.
brute.whySlow: String construction and set lookups add overhead.

optimal.idea: Weighted bidirectional adjacency: encode forward edges as weight 1 and reverse edges as weight 0, summing weights in O(n) DFS.
steps: Build adjacency list: for [u, v], add (v, 1) to adj[u] and (u, 0) to adj[v].
Run DFS from node 0 with parent parameter to avoid visited array.
For each (neighbor, cost): if neighbor != parent, add cost + dfs(neighbor, node).
Return total sum.

whyNext: Builds on reachability graph exploration from Course Schedule II (Seq 210) by interpreting jump offsets (i + arr[i] and i - arr[i]) as directed edges and searching for value 0 with BFS/DFS.
hints: From index i, you can jump to i + arr[i] or i - arr[i], provided the destination is within [0, arr.length - 1].
Treat this as a graph reachability problem from start node to any node with value 0.
Use BFS or DFS, marking visited indices (e.g. by negating arr[i]) to avoid infinite cycles. If arr[i] == 0 is reached, return true.

brute.idea: Standard DFS with a boolean visited array to explore left and right jumps.
steps: Create boolean[] visited.
Define dfs(idx): if out of bounds or visited[idx] return false.
If arr[idx] == 0 return true.
Mark visited[idx] = true, return dfs(idx + arr[idx]) || dfs(idx - arr[idx]).

optimal.idea: In-place array negation BFS: negate visited elements in arr to track visits without extra memory in O(n) time.
steps: Queue<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.offer(start);
While !q.isEmpty(): int cur = q.poll();
If arr[cur] == 0 return true; if arr[cur] < 0 continue;
int jump = arr[cur]; arr[cur] = -arr[cur];
If cur + jump < n q.offer(cur + jump); if cur - jump >= 0 q.offer(cur - jump);
Return false.

whyNext: Builds on bidirectional tree traversal from Reorder Routes (Seq 446) by returning subtree traversal times bottom-up, adding 2 seconds for each edge leading to a subtree containing at least one apple.
hints: Traverse the tree using bottom-up postorder DFS starting from node 0.
For each child subtree: if the child's subtree takes > 0 time, or if the child itself has an apple, the edge (parent, child) must be traversed back and forth (cost 2).
Total time = sum of (childTime + 2) for all children that either contain apples or have hasApple == true.

brute.idea: Find paths from root to every node with an apple, union all traversed edges into a set, and multiply set size by 2.
steps: Build undirected tree graph.
For each apple node, find the path from 0 to that node.
Add all edges on the path into a Set of undirected edges.
Return set.size() * 2.
brute.whySlow: Finding separate paths for every apple takes O(n * apples) time.

optimal.idea: Bottom-up postorder DFS: accumulate 2 units of time for every child edge that connects to an apple-containing subtree in O(n) time.
steps: Build adjacency list for undirected tree.
In dfs(node, parent): int total = 0.
For each neighbor in adj[node]: if neighbor != parent: childTime = dfs(neighbor, node); if childTime > 0 || hasApple[neighbor]: total += childTime + 2.
Return total.

whyNext: Builds on hierarchical tree recursion from Minimum Time to Collect All Apples in a Tree (Seq 448) by propagating manager informTime down to direct subordinates and finding the maximum path sum to any leaf.
hints: The employee hierarchy forms a directed tree with headID as root.
The time for an employee to receive news is the sum of informTime of all their managers up to the headID.
The total time needed is the maximum time taken to inform any employee: max path sum from root to leaf.

brute.idea: For every employee without subordinates (leaves), walk up the manager chain to root summing informTime, and take the maximum.
steps: Identify all leaves (employees who are not in the manager array).
For each leaf, follow manager pointers up to headID, summing informTime[manager].
Return the maximum time found across all leaves.
brute.whySlow: Tracing paths upwards repeatedly takes O(n * depth) time.

optimal.idea: Top-down DFS over adjacency tree: return informTime[node] + max(dfs(child)) in O(n) time.
steps: Build adjacency list: adj[manager[i]].add(i) for all i != headID.
Define dfs(node): if adj[node] is empty return 0.
maxSub = max(dfs(sub) for sub in adj[node]).
Return informTime[node] + maxSub.
Call dfs(headID) and return.

whyNext: Builds on flood fill connected components from Number of Islands (Seq 197) by flooding 0-cells from grid boundaries to eliminate open islands, then counting remaining isolated closed 0-islands surrounded entirely by 1s.
hints: A closed island consists of 0s (land) that cannot touch the boundary of the grid in any direction.
First pass: run flood fill on all 0-cells on the grid perimeter (first/last row and column) and turn them into 1s, since none of these can be closed.
Second pass: iterate through the internal grid; each unvisited 0-cell represents a verified closed island; flood fill it to 1 and increment the closed islands count.

brute.idea: Flood fill each 0-cell connected component and check whether any cell in the component touches the grid boundary.
steps: Create boolean visited[m][n].
For each (r, c) with grid[r][c] == 0 and not visited: run BFS/DFS.
Track boolean touchesBoundary = false.
If touchesBoundary is false, increment closed island count.
brute.whySlow: Allocates visited matrix and tracks boundary flags manually per component.

optimal.idea: Boundary flood fill pre-elimination: sink all perimeter-touching 0-cells to 1s, then count remaining internal 0-islands in O(m * n) time.
steps: Flood fill (dfs) all 0s on boundaries: top row, bottom row, left col, right col; convert 0s to 1s.
Loop internal cells (r from 1 to m - 2, c from 1 to n - 2): if grid[r][c] == 0, count++, dfs(r, c) to sink the island.
Return count.

whyNext: Builds on connected component flood fill from Number of Closed Islands (Seq 450) by traversing each island in grid2 and verifying that every single land cell is also land (1) in grid1.
hints: An island in grid2 is a sub-island if and only if EVERY cell of that island is also land (1) in grid1.
Traverse islands in grid2 using DFS/BFS, marking visited cells as 0.
Track a boolean isSub = true. During DFS of island in grid2, if grid1[r][c] == 0, set isSub = false. Continue DFS to completely sink the island in grid2 before checking isSub.

brute.idea: Find all cells of each grid2 island, then check if all collected cells are 1 in grid1.
steps: Use BFS to collect all coordinate pairs (r, c) of each island in grid2.
Check every collected cell: if any cell has grid1[r][c] == 0, island is not a sub-island.
Count qualifying sub-islands.
brute.whySlow: Allocates lists of coordinate pairs for every island.

optimal.idea: In-place boolean DFS sinking: sink grid2 island in-place, returning false if any constituent cell lacks grid1 land in O(m * n) time.
steps: In dfs(r, c): if out of bounds or grid2[r][c] == 0 return true.
grid2[r][c] = 0.
boolean isSub = grid1[r][c] == 1.
Recurse in 4 directions, combining results with bitwise & (to avoid short-circuiting so entire island is sunk).
Return isSub & down & up & right & left.

whyNext: Builds on multi-source BFS from 01 Matrix (Seq 204) by enqueueing all land cells (1) simultaneously and expanding outward level by level to find the water cell with maximum Manhattan distance.
hints: If the grid contains all land (1s) or all water (0s), there is no valid distance; return -1.
Enqueue all land cells (1s) into a BFS queue simultaneously with distance 0.
Expand outward in 4 directions, marking visited water cells as visited; the number of BFS levels expanded before the queue empties is the maximum distance.

brute.idea: For every water cell (0), compute Manhattan distance to every land cell (1), find the min, and maximize across water cells.
steps: Collect coordinates of all 1s (land) and all 0s (water).
If either list is empty, return -1.
For each water cell, find min distance to any land cell.
Return maximum min distance.
brute.whySlow: Comparing every water cell to every land cell takes O((m*n)^2) time.

optimal.idea: Multi-source BFS from land cells: expand BFS wavefront level by level, returning the number of levels expanded in O(n^2) time.
steps: Queue<int[]> q = new LinkedList<>().
Add all land cells (value 1) into q.
If q.size() == 0 || q.size() == n * n return -1.
int dist = -1; while (!q.isEmpty()): dist++; int sz = q.size(); repeat sz times: pop cell, explore 4 neighbors; if neighbor in bounds and grid == 0: grid = 1, q.offer(neighbor).
Return dist.

whyNext: Builds on shortest path unweighted grid BFS from Shortest Path in Binary Matrix (Seq 205) by identifying border boundary cells (r == 0, r == m-1, c == 0, c == n-1) as exits, excluding the entrance itself.
hints: Use BFS starting at the entrance cell with step count 0.
An exit is any '.' cell on the border of the maze (row 0 or m-1, or col 0 or n-1) that is NOT the entrance.
Mark visited cells as '+' immediately when pushed to queue to avoid duplicate processing. Return steps on first valid border exit hit.

brute.idea: Find all border exit coordinates first, then run BFS to find the shortest distance from entrance to any exit.
steps: Scan border cells to collect all candidate exits (excluding entrance).
If no candidate exits exist, return -1.
Run BFS from entrance until any collected exit is popped.
Return steps.
brute.whySlow: Preprocessing exits and set lookups add overhead.

optimal.idea: Direct BFS boundary exit detection: return steps + 1 as soon as any neighboring empty cell touches the grid boundary in O(m * n) time.
steps: Let m = maze.length, n = maze[0].length.
Queue<int[]> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.offer(new int[]{entrance[0], entrance[1]});
maze[entrance[0]][entrance[1]] = '+'; int steps = 0;
While !q.isEmpty(): sz = q.size(); steps++; repeat sz times: pop [r, c], for 4 neighbors: if in bounds and '.': if border cell return steps; maze[nr][nc] = '+'; q.offer([nr, nc]).
Return -1.

whyNext: Builds on grid neighbor inspection from Nearest Exit in Maze (Seq 453) by revealing clicked mines ('M' -> 'X'), counting 8-directional adjacent mines, or recursively revealing blank squares ('E' -> 'B').
hints: If click is an unrevealed mine 'M', change it to 'X' and return immediately.
If click is an unrevealed empty square 'E': count adjacent mines in all 8 directions.
If adjacent mine count > 0: set board[r][c] to (char) ('0' + count) and stop. If count == 0: set board[r][c] = 'B' and recursively reveal all 8 unrevealed 'E' neighbors.

brute.idea: BFS revelation: queue clicked square, count adjacent mines, expand if 0 mines.
steps: If click is 'M', change to 'X' and return.
Add click to queue.
While queue not empty: pop cell, count adjacent mines.
If count > 0, set digit. If 0, set 'B' and enqueue unrevealed neighbors.
Return board.
brute.whySlow: Queue handling adds allocation overhead compared to direct DFS recursion.

optimal.idea: Recursive DFS reveal: directly update board cells in 8 directions when adjacent mine count is 0 in O(m * n) time.
steps: int r = click[0], c = click[1].
If board[r][c] == 'M': board[r][c] = 'X'; return board.
In dfs(r, c): count adjacent mines.
If mines > 0: board[r][c] = (char) ('0' + mines); return.
board[r][c] = 'B'; for each 8 neighbors: if neighbor == 'E' dfs(nr, nc).
Return board.

whyNext: Builds on board state BFS navigation from Minesweeper (Seq 454) by converting Boustrophedon board numbers (1 to n^2) into 2D row/col coordinates and finding minimum dice rolls with BFS.
hints: Square numbers 1 to n^2 alternate direction row-by-row starting from the bottom row.
Coordinate conversion: row from top is n - 1 - (s - 1) / n. If that row from bottom is odd, col is (s - 1) % n; otherwise n - 1 - (s - 1) % n.
Run standard unweighted BFS from square 1. For each square s, branch to s + 1 through min(s + 6, n^2); if destination has a snake or ladder (board[r][c] != -1), destination jumps to board[r][c].

brute.idea: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm over the n^2 state graph.
steps: Initialize distances array dist with infinity.
Priority queue stores (dist, square).
Pop smallest dist, explore next 1-6 dice moves.
Return dist[n*n].
brute.whySlow: Priority queue adds O(log V) overhead compared to standard FIFO BFS queue.

optimal.idea: Unweighted BFS on 1..n^2: each dice roll has uniform weight 1, so BFS guarantees the minimum moves in O(n^2) time.
steps: Map square s to (r, c) using boustrophedon index arithmetic.
boolean[] visited = new boolean[n * n + 1]; Queue<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>();
q.offer(1); visited[1] = true; int moves = 0;
While !q.isEmpty(): sz = q.size(); moves++; for each square: try rolls 1 to 6; jump snake/ladder if present; if dest == n*n return moves; if !visited[dest] visited[dest] = true, q.offer(dest).
Return -1.

whyNext: Builds on multi-state BFS from Snakes and Ladders (Seq 455) by tracking vertex visitations paired with edge color (0 for red, 1 for blue) to enforce strict color alternation.
hints: A node can be visited multiple times as long as it is entered via different edge colors.
State representation in BFS: (node, lastColor) where color 0 = red and 1 = blue.
Initialize queue with (0, 0) and (0, 1) at distance 0. If lastColor was red, only traverse blue outgoing edges; if blue, only traverse red outgoing edges.

brute.idea: Run separate BFS for each destination node from root 0 tracking alternating colors.
steps: For each destination i from 0 to n - 1: run alternating BFS from 0 to i.
Store shortest path length in ans[i].
Return ans array.
brute.whySlow: Running n separate BFS searches takes O(n * (V + E)) time.

optimal.idea: Single multi-state BFS: 2 states per node (node, color) finds shortest alternating paths to all nodes in O(V + E) time.
steps: Build red and blue adjacency lists.
int[] ans = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(ans, -1).
boolean[][] vis = new boolean[n][2]; Queue<int[]> q = new LinkedList<>();
Enqueue (0, 0) and (0, 1); vis[0][0] = vis[0][1] = true; steps = 0;
While !q.isEmpty(): level iteration; if ans[node] == -1 ans[node] = steps; expand alternating edges; steps++.
Return ans.

whyNext: Builds on BFS graph traversal from Shortest Path with Alternating Colors (Seq 456) by grouping identical values into a HashMap and clearing each value's index list upon first exploration to avoid O(n^2) edge explosion.
hints: From index i, valid moves are i + 1, i - 1, and any index j where arr[i] == arr[j].
Map each unique number to a list of its indices in a HashMap<Integer, List<Integer>>.
CRITICAL: after exploring all indices with value arr[i], immediately clear the list in the map: map.get(arr[i]).clear() to prevent quadratic revisits.

brute.idea: Standard BFS exploring all neighbors without clearing mapped value lists.
steps: Map values to index lists.
BFS from index 0.
Explore i-1, i+1, and all j where arr[j] == arr[i].
Return steps to reach n - 1.
brute.whySlow: When all elements have identical values, repeatedly scanning the list takes O(n^2) time.

optimal.idea: BFS with cleared value buckets: clear the bucket in the map once traversed, guaranteeing O(n) linear execution time.
steps: Build Map<Integer, List<Integer>> graph.
boolean[] visited = new boolean[n]; visited[0] = true; Queue<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.offer(0);
int steps = 0; while (!q.isEmpty()): int sz = q.size();
For each node: if node == n - 1 return steps; check node - 1 and node + 1; check graph[arr[node]]; then graph.get(arr[node]).clear();
steps++; Return steps.

whyNext: Builds on directed graph reachability from Course Schedule (Seq 212) by creating a directed edge i -> j if bomb i's blast radius covers bomb j's center, finding the start bomb that maximizes DFS reachability.
hints: Bomb i can detonate bomb j if Euclidean distance squared <= radius_i^2: (x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2 <= r1^2.
Notice this relation is directed: bomb i might reach bomb j, but bomb j might have a smaller radius and not reach bomb i.
Build a directed adjacency list. Run DFS/BFS from every bomb i to count the total reachable bombs, and return the maximum count.

brute.idea: Build directed graph and run BFS from every node, tracking maximum reachable count.
steps: For each pair (i, j): if distSq <= r[i]^2, add edge i -> j.
Run BFS from every node i.
Count visited nodes for each BFS run.
Return maximum count.
brute.whySlow: Straightforward O(n * (V + E)) = O(n^3) graph search.

optimal.idea: Directed adjacency list with bitset/DFS exploration: compute reachability component size for each node in O(n^3) time.
steps: Precalculate directed adjacency list using 64-bit squared distance check.
For each bomb i from 0 to n - 1: initialize boolean[] vis, call dfs(i) counting reached nodes.
Track max detonation count.
Return max count.
